g.text: Freezing the bucket ranges is what keeps 'which arm was this user in' a FACT, not a function of when you ask
Every table, index and consistency choice traces back to one question: is the gap real, or did we just get unlucky about who saw what?
bucket_start / bucket_end are computed ONCE and
FROZEN the instant the experiment starts
the 'do not break this' list, checked
the durable record of who was actually SERVED what
the ONLY table the analysis path touches
so there is no consistency question to answer
The volume gap between those two blue tables is the whole sharding story: millions
of exposure events a day against about 1.35 million total live summary rows. The
same 'raw event volume dwarfs its own aggregate' shape as ad-click aggregation
Both shard by experiment_id - matching the dominant query for each ('this
experiment's exposures', 'this experiment's metric curve') and, just as
importantly, keeping the (experiment_id, user_id) UNIQUENESS CONSTRAINT
ENFORCEABLE WITHIN A SINGLE SHARD rather than needing a cross-shard check.
Sharding either by a hash of user_id instead would scatter one experiment's
population across every shard, turning both the join AND the dedup check into
And the replica-versus-shard distinction, again: replicas solve read throughput
for reporting and ad hoc audit queries against exposures; sharding solves the
write volume and total size of exposures itself. Reaching for one when the other
is the actual bottleneck is the mistake to avoid.
The single most important modelling decision in this schema
a FEATURE FLAG grows a rollout range: 10% -> 20%
users already inside the range keep their bucket;
only the new edge adds users <- the whole point
an EXPERIMENT whose ranges shift mid-run
a user drifts from control's range into treatment's;
both behaviours attribute to whichever arm fired <- contamination
It is the same hash-boundary-shift mechanic in both cases, and a feature-flag rollout leans on it INTENTIONALLY: growing a
range only adds users at the new edge, never reassigns users already inside it. For an experiment, that same behaviour means a
user's behaviour under control AND their behaviour under treatment both get attributed to whichever arm they happened to be in
when a conversion event fired - contaminating the exact comparison the system exists to make.
So bucket_start and bucket_end are computed once, from the allocation percentages in effect the moment start is called, and
never touched again for that experiment. Same technique, opposite verdict, from one differing requirement.
Same duplicate-delivery problem as ad clicks; different mechanism, and it is worth naming why
ad click a short-TTL dedup cache
the window only needs to outlive its allowed-lateness
an exposure a durable UNIQUE(experiment_id, user_id)
has to stay deduplicated for the ENTIRE RUN -
days to weeks - and is worth keeping permanently
An exposure is a fact worth keeping for audit and later re-analysis, not something safe to let expire. A durable unique
constraint gives the identical 'first exposure wins, everything after is a no-op' guarantee as a payments idempotency key, at
the timescale this table's data actually needs. It is also, simultaneously, the index every join in the aggregator uses to ask
'has this user already been exposed to this experiment?'
Indexes - each one matching exactly one query that actually runs
experiments(status, started_at) 'which experiments are currently running' - the query every scheduled
analysis sweep and every guardrail cycle runs. The same (status, timestamp)
composite reasoning as the job scheduler's due-jobs scan.
experiment_variants(experiment_id) every assignment-config load and every analysis run reads all of one
experiment's variants together. No index on variant_key alone, because it is
UNIQUE exposures(experiment_id, user_id) the concurrency-safety mechanism above, doubling as the aggregator's join
summaries(experiment_id, variant_key, the COMPOSITE PRIMARY KEY, matching ad-click aggregation's (ad_id,
metric_name, day) window_start) reasoning exactly: the dominant read is 'this experiment's
per-variant metric curve over time', so the key itself serves the query with
no secondary index. experiment_id FIRST is the leftmost-prefix point - it is
what lets a single-experiment read jump straight to its rows without
srm_checks(experiment_id, checked_at) 'this experiment's most recent SRM check' - the only pattern that ever runs
Consistency - and one 'eventual' that is a mechanism rather than a limitation
the SDK's entire correctness rests on every instance agreeing on the same frozen bucket ranges. A read that is even
briefly stale in the wrong direction - one instance still using pre-freeze ranges - would put some users in a different
variant than others computing the identical hash a moment later.
strong at WRITE time, replica-friendly for reads
the unique-constraint check has to be atomic, for the same reason a payment's idempotency key does. But an internal audit
pulling one experiment's full exposure list is a legitimate replica read: replication lag does not change who was actually
exposed, only how promptly an ad hoc query reflects the very latest exposure.
a row becomes visible only once the aggregator has joined that day's exposures against conversions inside the attribution
window and the peeking gate has decided a read is even appropriate. This is not imprecision being tolerated - WAITING IS
THE MECHANISM THAT MAKES THE EVENTUAL NUMBER MORE CORRECT, by giving late conversions their full window before anything is
there is no update path, so there is no consistency question.
